extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, early scientists and practitioners (mapmakers, geologists, astronomers, anatomists, physicians, horticulturalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for observing, classifying, mapping, experimenting, and reporting natural-philosophy/medical/horticultural phenomena (maps of soils, classification of sands and clays, experimental reports, eclipse timing, anatomical dissections, clinical letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil/mineral map composition and labelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The soil or mineral map should be distinguished into countries, with the rivers and some of the noted towns put in; the soil might either be coloured by a variety of lines or etchings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'The same map of England may, for want of a better, at present serve the turn. It might be distinguished into countries, with the rivers and some of the noted towns put in. The soil might either be coloured by a variety of lines or etchings; but great care must be taken very exactly to note on the map, where such and such soils are bounded.' Emphasises inclusion of political/topographic reference points and explicit, precise boundaries for soil types; use distinct graphic conventions (colours, lines, etchings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map purpose — record extent and limits of soils
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps should note how far soil types extend and the limits of each soil so that from the whole and from every part further inference may be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Now if it were noted how far these extended, and the limits of each soil appeared on a map, something more might be comprehended from the whole, and from every part, than I can possibly foresee.' Use maps to enable geological inference by explicitly recording spatial extent and boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sand classification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify sands by texture (sharp/rag, fine, coarse, soft/smooth), colour, calcination behaviour, presence of mica/glitter, provenance (mountain, sea), and suitability for uses (e.g., glass-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from table: 'Sharp or rag sand, composed of small transparent pebbles, naturally found upon the mountains, not calcinable.' 'Fine — White... Calice sand, burns reddish...' 'With mica of glittering particles... Gold-like; A vein of mica...' Use tactile/visual tests and burning/calcination to distinguish types and note localities and industrial uses (glass, cementing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clay classification and descriptive standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe clays by consistency (pure/soft like butter, greasy), grittiness, colour, calcination/stone character (stony when dry), mixture with sand/pebbles, presence of mica, and local occurrence; note uses (pottery, medicinal earths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table entries: 'Pure, that is, such as is soft like butter to the teeth... Greasy, to be reckoned among the medicinal earths...' 'Stony, when dry.' Provide locality examples (Wakefield Moor potter's clay, Isle of Wight milk-white clay) and link properties to uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and documentation of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental reports should be organised under clear heads/topics, describe instruments used, and record experiments systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Academy del Cimento: 'The experiments are comprised under 10 heads, treating of several subjects. Having described some of their instruments, as thermometers... the pendulum, and other instruments.' Emphasises explicit instrument description, topical organisation (air pressure, freezing, magnetism, etc.), and comprehensive recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rigor — repeatability, answering objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments should be repeated, objections anticipated and answered, and both animate and inanimate cases examined where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'They come then to their first head, the air's pressure; where most of the known mercurial experiments are tried and confirmed, objections answered, &c. with several experiments made in vacuo, both on animate and inanimate bodies.' Reports should state confirmations and responses to criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of instruments and measurement calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe instruments in detail and standardise/reduce measurements to a standard so results are comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: thermometers and pendulum described and 'reduced to a standard' in Academy del Cimento. Also for eclipse timing: use solar altitudes to correct clocks. Include instrument provenance and calibration procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical timing accuracy (clock correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure timing of observations is accurate by correcting clocks through independent celestial measurements (e.g., taking solar altitudes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From eclipse report: 'The true times of the same were observed... by taking some altitudes of the sun to correct the clocks.' Use astronomical methods to calibrate local timekeepers before recording event times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance publication of predicted events to enable observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish predicted times/ephemerides of astronomical events in advance so observers can prepare to observe accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Flamsteed: 'predictions of the eclipses of Jupiter's satellites... containing a list of the times, nearly when they might be expected to happen in the year following; that astronomers might be apprised of the times when to prepare for observing them more accurately.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for anatomical discovery and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Anatomical claims should be based on direct dissection, clear description of techniques (e.g., probing), illustrated figures, and confirmation by observations in multiple specimens/species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From salivary-duct note: discovery by probing during dissection ('Searching with a probe... he slipped it... into this duct') and 'This discovery was afterwards confirmed by observations made on other animals, such as sheep, the bear, and a lioness.' Provide labelled figures showing glands, ducts, orifices and probe positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical case-reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical/clinical letters should include date and place, patient details (age/occupation when relevant), precise description of symptoms and signs, interventions performed, and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: letters dated (e.g., 'dated London, Aug. 4, 1684'), description of conditions ('bursa oculi... a bag... on the white of the eye'), interventions ('I applied a cupping-glass... scarified, and cupped him again... put on a plaster of diapalma'), and results ('he was perfectly cured'). Include notable unusual phenomena (stones from impostume, magnet to remove iron in iris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Horticultural/practical guidance should be experience-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical manuals (e.g., on pruning fruit trees) should present rules derived from long experience for cultivation, ordering of trees, and uses/management of fruits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'The Art of pruning Fruit Trees': 'gives here the rules which many years experience has taught him on those subjects, viz. the cultivation and ordering of the trees, with the uses and management of the fruits.' Emphasise concrete, practice-oriented rules and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological inference supported by multiple observational lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing geological hypotheses (e.g., origin/distribution of sand), support claims with multiple lines of evidence: distribution on mountains, river transport, seashore occurrences, stratigraphic relations beneath peat/moss, and physical properties (hardness/durability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's arguments: rivers bring sand from mountains; sea-shores barred with sand; sandy sea-grounds; sand under moss beds indicating long-term deposition; sand's hardness/durableness suggests ancient widespread cover. Use distributional, transport, stratigraphic, and material-property evidence together to argue origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-history observation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise locations, seasonal visibility, spatial extent (e.g., 'for the space of 40 yards in length, and about 10 in breadth'), qualitative and quantitative properties (degree of saltness), experimental tests (e.g., boiling brine), and reasoned inferences about origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salt-spring example: 'It rises in the middle of the River Wear... only to be seen and tasted in the summer time... seems to bubble up equally in all parts of the channel, for the space of 40 yards in length, and about 10 in breadth... the saltest of all the springs issues out of the middle of a rock... though but little in quantity in comparison of the fresh river, yet of that force as to give a brackishness to the streams 100 yards below.' Include sensory tests (taste), simple experiments (boiling to produce bay salt), and spatial measurements.
